text: I'm Senior UX designer at SAP Concur - currently worked on our platform UX team
Platform is sign in and some admin configuration areas to set up different functionality
Previously worked for about seven, eight years on expense product - our flagship product
Designing new features and helping transition from old ASP pages with old design language to new UI pages built on node and react
Much more modern than 25 year old technology
I design what's on the screen - not the code behind it but how it looks, how it feels, how it flows
To make that end to end experience of you trying to complete a task as easy to use, as intuitive as possible
You have a document you want to print - you hit the print button - where's that? Up in the toolbar
How do you know which one's the print button - well it's got the little printer icon
Where are they going to look, what icon, do we need to put the word there, where else would you look
What do you expect to happen - you start printing or get some options
Which options - all the options or just the most common options
We're trying to make that as easy and as simple - not overwhelm you but give you what you need
Our goal is really you don't even think about it, you just do it
If somebody asked what was that experience and they're like 'it's fine I printed it, what's the big deal' - that's a great design
The main value is understanding
The user experience is from the moment your customer hears about your product to updating it, migrating to the next version
That whole end to end journey is the user experience
Most people think of user experience as I start the program and I sign in - that's the beginning of user experience - it's not
Some people call that customer experience - I think that's fine, want to call it whatever you want
I think of a Venn diagram in software - the development team experts in what we can build
There's the product team, the PMs, and they focus on what's the right thing for the business
This may be something we can build, maybe super useful to users, but it makes no sense for us as a company to build
A music app - why would we build a music app? People like to listen to music while filling out expense report - no that doesn't make sense for us
UX understands what the user is trying to accomplish, their expectations, where they're coming from, their points of reference
How to research that, understand that, get that feedback to make sure the business decision and the development actually building it lands well with the end user
It's a product that people can use and they enjoy using, they like using it
If they don't like it you're not going to get great sales
I hear leadership talking about 'oh yeah UX is super important, they need to be involved in everything' - great, we don't have enough headcount to do that
I am seeing people put their money where their mouth is - there's new people added like every other week which is fantastic
It's been a lot of lip service - 'oh UX is really important' - okay well then we need to slow down and do some user research
We really need to shove this out the door next quarter because we already promised it to these key customers - we don't have time for proper design and research
I thought you said UX was important - oh yeah yeah totally it's totally important - but...
There's teams that haven't had the resources, they're inexperienced and don't understand the value - that's totally understandable
One of the big things we need to do as UX is demonstrate and explain what the value is that we bring to the table
It's super easy for PM and dev to get so deep in the weeds on technology that they say 'just surface that'
If you were an engineer who worked on it that would totally work - you're not selling it to engineers who worked on it
You're trying to do this - does it do A, B or C? You're telling me about migrating backend - who cares? What are you telling me this for?
Nobody's going to understand that - we need to think about this from the end user standpoint, that's the real value we bring
I use Figma, I use Figma Make which is their AI thing which has very little to do with actual AI
I use Gemini and ChatGPT on almost a daily basis
If I'm writing an email to external people I want to make sure I'm being professional - I'll have it read through what I wrote
Hey can you help me phrase this in a way that's more team oriented and not me oriented
When I'm on calls with people I'm just having Gemini create a transcript that I can go back to
It's not fantastic but it's better than me trying to type out notes
I use it on almost an everyday basis
It saves me time
I can write up what I think, how I feel, and somebody on the other end takes it a bit too personal or too direct
I can write it out how I want to, hey can you soften this a bit, be a bit more professional - boom it's done
I don't have to sit there and go how can I phrase this, is this going to come across as abrasive
I can be blunt, I can write it exactly how I want to, and then make it be the professional version
I save so much time having it correct grammar
That transcript from Gemini - I don't have to sit there and type out what everybody said
I see other people especially like project managers and product managers using it - our PMs use it for writing requirements
The content writers on our team use it for content writing and editing
To make the leap to I can do your job for you - that's a bit wild
A lot of people don't actually understand what UX does - they think it's just make it pretty
Well you can do that with AI - sure some of it
The understanding and empathy for end users - AI is not going to be able to do that
To the layman it looks like 'oh we can replace this' when in reality it's just a tool we're using to do our job faster
It can do a lot, there's a lot of value that it has, but it's not the savior
It's not magic, it's a tool, it's another tool in the tool belt
The perception and the hype and the marketing has made it seem like it's the second coming
I don't think the work has really changed that much - I'm still doing the same things I was doing before
We have access to better tools
It makes my life easier to get to the output that's needed
It doesn't fundamentally change what we're trying to accomplish
What I'm concerned about is people not understanding what we actually do, what the value is, and they're looking to save a dollar
Now we have this magic thing that supposedly can do this - well we can save money, we don't need to hire as many UX people
I'm a UX design specialist at SAP Concur working on the Concur Travel product
Before this I was at a smaller startup doing product design for a healthcare application
I've been in UX for about six years now
I design the user interface and experience for business travel booking and management
Making sure employees can book flights, hotels, rental cars in a way that's efficient and meets company policy
It's a complex domain because you're balancing user needs with corporate requirements
UX is about understanding what people are trying to do and making that as smooth as possible
It's research, it's design, it's testing - making sure what we build actually works for the people using it
A good design is one where users don't notice the design - they just accomplish what they came to do
I think the company values UX - we have a decent sized team and we're included in most product decisions
There's always the challenge of timelines - sometimes we don't get as much research time as we'd like
But overall I feel like UX has a seat at the table
I use ChatGPT pretty regularly for writing and ideation
If I'm writing user research summaries or documentation I'll use it to help structure my thoughts
I'll also use it for brainstorming - like if I'm stuck on how to approach a design problem
I don't use AI for actual design work - I still do that in Figma myself
It helps me work faster on the writing and thinking parts
I can draft something quickly and then refine it instead of staring at a blank page
It's like having a thought partner to bounce ideas off of
I see product managers using it a lot for writing product requirements and user stories
Developers use it for code generation and debugging
I think most people on my team use ChatGPT or similar tools at least occasionally
I think some people see AI tools as more capable than they actually are
There's this idea that AI can just design things for you - but it really can't
It can help with certain tasks but you still need the human judgment and creativity
My day to day work hasn't changed dramatically
I'm still doing research, design, working with stakeholders
The main difference is I have a tool that helps me with certain parts of the process
Writing is faster, brainstorming is easier
But the core UX work is the same
I don't think it changes my value as a designer
The value I bring is understanding users, solving complex problems, making strategic design decisions
AI can help with execution but it doesn't replace the thinking
I could see how someone who doesn't understand UX might think AI could replace designers
If you think design is just making things look nice then yeah maybe AI could do that
But that's not what UX is
The research, the strategy, the user understanding - AI isn't doing that
I think the role will evolve but not disappear
We'll probably spend less time on certain tasks and more time on higher level thinking
Maybe less time writing docs and more time on research and strategy
I think the skills that will matter are the ones AI can't do
Empathy, critical thinking, understanding context and nuance
Being able to work with stakeholders and navigate organizational dynamics
Those are the things that make a designer valuable
I'm generally positive about AI
I see it as a tool that makes my work easier in some ways
I'm not worried about it replacing me because I understand what I actually do
I think the concerns about AI replacing designers are overblown
The biggest value UX brings is understanding the user deeply
That comes from research, from talking to people, from observing how they work
You can't automate empathy
I've been recognized for my work on a major redesign project
That recognition was based on the research insights and strategic thinking I brought
Not about how fast I could produce designs
In travel booking there's a lot of complexity - different booking types, policies, approval workflows
Figuring out how to make that understandable and easy to use is the challenge
AI isn't going to understand our users' mental models or what makes sense in this context
I spend a lot of time in user research - interviews, usability testing, analyzing data

sub: AI assists but cannot replace research
text: AI can help me analyze transcripts or summarize findings but it can't do the actual research
It can't ask follow-up questions or pick up on non-verbal cues
Working with stakeholders is a big part of my job
Getting alignment, managing expectations, explaining design decisions
That's all human interaction and relationship building
I use AI maybe 30% of my workday
Mostly for writing tasks - documentation, emails, summaries
The other 70% is meetings, design work, research - things AI doesn't help with
I think some companies might try to reduce headcount based on AI promises
That would be a mistake because they'd lose the actual value UX provides
But I don't think that's happening at my company
If anything we're hiring more UX people
I think leadership sees the value we bring
The way I use AI is similar to how I'd use a junior designer
I give it direction, it gives me a starting point, then I refine and make the final decisions
But it's not as good as a junior designer because it doesn't learn or understand context the same way
I don't think design education needs to change dramatically because of AI
The fundamentals are still the fundamentals - research methods, design thinking, user psychology
Maybe add some training on how to use AI tools effectively
The hard skills are still important - knowing how to use design tools, understanding visual design principles
But the soft skills are probably more important - communication, collaboration, critical thinking
I'm curious to see how AI develops
I think it will get better at certain tasks
But I don't think it will fundamentally change what makes a good designer
The best designers will be the ones who can use AI as a tool while still bringing their own creativity and judgment
I've seen some designers who are resistant to AI and I think that's a mistake
It's a tool that can make you more efficient - why wouldn't you use it
I think the narrative around AI replacing jobs is overblown in general
It's more about augmenting than replacing
At least in design, I don't see how AI could fully replace what we do
My manager values the strategic thinking I bring to projects
The ability to see the big picture and connect design decisions to business goals
I collaborate with product managers daily
We work together to define requirements and prioritize features
That's a lot of discussion and negotiation - very human work
I present my designs to stakeholders and explain the rationale
Being able to tell the story and get buy-in is crucial
AI can't do that for me
I think about the user journey across multiple touchpoints
Understanding how different parts of the experience connect
That requires context and judgment that AI doesn't have
Sometimes I prototype in code to test interactions
I could see AI helping with that - generating code for simple interactions
That would save time
I'm involved in hiring for UX roles
What we look for is problem-solving ability, communication skills, portfolio showing strategic thinking
Not just visual polish but the thinking behind the work
I don't think AI changes what makes a good design hire
If anything it makes the human skills more important
Overall I'm optimistic about the future of UX
I think the role is secure and will continue to be important
AI will change some things but not the fundamental value of good design
I see AI as an opportunity not a threat
It lets me focus on the work I find most interesting and valuable
Less time on tedious tasks, more time on creative problem-solving
I think the key is to stay adaptable
Learn new tools, but don't lose sight of the fundamentals
The core of design is understanding people and solving their problems
That's not going to change

Having a user centric mindset was the core value
After working I don't think anyone really cares about that

I was in the strategy and partnership team of the company on a SaaS-based product for qualitative researchers
The product was mainly for researchers and organizations that want qualitative data - our tool helped them annotate documents
Tools of similar capabilities like Dovetail and NVivo had all introduced new AI features at that time
Even though AI wasn't giving what researchers fully wanted, it was still reducing a lot of tasks they had to do manually
Clients wanted our tool to have AI features similar to competitors - they wanted AI inspirations
I interviewed clients to understand what kind of pain points they had when using our tool
I tried to find at what touch points we could intervene or introduce AI features to reduce client workload
After five to six interactions with the client we clearly understood what they need - they often don't know what they need
Sometimes they feel data is important but don't know if it's quant or qualitative or just a survey
We basically had to consult them - these are not the requirements, these are your requirements
We had to make them understand what annotation tags are and the difference between manual and automatic annotation
The product team gave us three platforms: staging, design platform, and production platform
In staging we set up all the tools and that's where we could play around and show clients what we planned
After client changes we integrate it with a WhatsApp chatbot
I come from industrial and product design background - I used to go and spend time with people who practice things and observe
I started to recognize client patterns in two to three calls - they always spoke in terms of monetization
I worked in manufacturing for a while - it was too restricted to work in that environment
When I was working on the SaaS product every thought process had to be thinking in terms of research
Did you think from all directions - strategically or product feasibility or tried to solve from all the things you know
When I joined my first internship that's when Midjourney and ChatGPT were both introduced
When I was in the industry it was still early to use AI because there were a lot of things it could do wrong
Most of the times we end up picking our friends or somebody closely in touch as users - we don't get real data
There's a lot of thought process given towards okay is this really a problem or not - and a lot of things are not considered
That never happens because many companies are focused towards monetizing - they want profit and traction to run
They use all the hacks and things to make sure they get profit - making products addictive and bringing in more users
Companies want us to recognize patterns - either try to hack it and bring in more users or make the product more addictive
I initially used to think companies care too much about users and UX designers are brought in to understand user pain points
Now I have realized that's not what the companies want - it's mainly about companies wanting us to recognize patterns
Clients always speak in terms of monetization - what is in this for us, how can this tool help us monetize
I had to tell them you can use this to market yourself and bring in customers and people who are ready to invest
That's when they started getting to understand where the tool would really help them
All they used to ask was how much time does your users spend on this page
Are they really going to click the link or not - that was the main thing companies cared about

sub: Practical CTA design for early brands
text: If you're designing for a brand that is still budding follow the principle of highlighting things and making one main CTA
Making sure there is only one button on the screen on every swipe - one main focus call to action
Every button should speak the same language - not something says subscribe now and something says buy now
Everything should be structured so the user knows if I press this I'm getting that product
I worked in manufacturing and I don't think they had any understanding about what UX is or what value a UX designer brings
For them it was about keeping the machine running so that everything is fast paced - design was subordinate to throughput
Design meant just go to Google search and try to replicate things - whatever is trending just copy that
Don't be too creative - I don't think they expected creativity either, they expected copying
None of them were designers - even the head was not a designer in the manufacturing part
For them it was all about engineering and whatever is possible in that machine constraint
A lot of things in the program are only focused on making our thing look beautiful or fascinating or different from others
Speaking in terms of program and the kinds of projects we get - a lot of things is lost in terms of UX
I want to observe and understand and do ethnographic research - they might be doing things involuntarily that we need to observe
Now here everything has become digital - limiting the observation-based methods I learned from industrial design
The value of UX is to think from exactly a human perspective and design for that
Or think in terms of monetization but also not compromising the user's ethics and values
One side is where ethics come into picture - you need to be more careful and consider all kinds of people
There should be no one that has to be excluded - projects should be inclusive
It should also be immersive experience - not something just you see on a screen and that's all
The other part is design strategy - most things are related to what is the company going to benefit from this

sub: Real client projects in design strategy
text: We had clients like Superhuman and some other startups - both sides of UX and strategic design were experienced
One is an ideal design with no constraints no restrictions if we were supposed to consider only UX principles

sub: Strategic design balancing company and user
text: As a strategic designer thinking in strategic way what all things we need to consider to benefit the company rather than just the user
I get recognized mainly for getting teams to align - lot of the time we lose track and deviate from the brief
I always try to stick to the brief and what is given and not go too deviated from that
I do good sketching and prototypes and all these things - that's my strength
I automatically get assigned to prototyping and sketching roles - also a bit of presentation work
I'm a little particular - I want things to be in the right order and done in my specific way
In documentation if people use some random font structured very randomly for me it's okay what am I doing here
When I try to change documentation they give feedback that I changed it without letting them know
I had professors who spent 60-70 years in design and they all had their own ethics and values
They would say I am never designing for a corporate company - only for people who are part of the less economy
Their no would also be very loud and clear - they would not work for corporate companies and had strong professional values

sub: Design strategy vs pure UX tension
text: Design problems are about designing a tool or product but business problems are solving actual market or monetization problems

I use Claude to schedule my budget - I think I used Claude to plan my grocery too
I just added all the items that I had with me and asked Claude do I need to shop groceries and it said no for four weeks
Because I had asked it to generate a diet plan it understood what kind of diet I was doing and connected that to groceries
Every week I had to spend only $2 on fruits - apart from that I had everything stocked and didn't know
I also ask Claude to give me a tracker for body weight and whether I'm drinking water properly and eating before six
But I never went back and used it - so that's kind of funny
I structure my prompts so that sometimes I wanted to think from all directions - sometimes I just want the approach
Sometimes I just tell it I don't want you to do things - I just want you to give me the approach
I use a format where I describe the problem and give it a task section - this is the task I want, not anything else

In your previous project you did all these things - I was like I want a fresh start but Gemini keeps doing this
I don't think Claude does that - it doesn't inappropriately bring in previous conversation context

For me AI is helping - even as a designer I might not know exactly what to do but it's assisting me towards that direction
I feel like it's a tool that you have to learn and use - it's there, you either use it or you rant about it

My boss said use Midjourney - why are you thinking too much in terms of ideations, generate concepts and then build on it

sub: Unofficial AI use in restricted courses
text: Unofficially we do use it - but what I do is look into what it generates and understand and come back from my own perspective
Try to come back and work on the same thing from my understanding and my perspective - taking inspirations but not entirely sticking to it
Even though a little bit here and there I might take inspirations but not entirely sticking to what it has generated

sub: Observed covert AI use in class
text: I've seen people use it for the course anyway - so it's not fully prevented by the guidelines

sub: Faculty using AI for student feedback

sub: Harm narrative around AI in education
text: It's like oh it's doing this it's doing that it's doing a lot of harm - but it's about how people use it

sub: Use AI or fall behind framing
text: You either can use it and try to be current to the generation or you can just rant about it and be left behind

sub: Classroom mood deflated by AI negativity
text: Always speaking about the negatives of it kind of brings the classroom vibe a little bit off

sub: Faculty want students to learn by doing
text: For them who have looked into all parts of their experience as designers they want us to learn
They want us to experience that learning or try to go with the process
This thing reduces the time by so much - faculty may feel like students are not learning anything
I think they want us to learn rather than just try to get things done - AI enables task completion over learning

Restricting them not to use it is making them use it more somewhere else

sub: Faculty believe AI output is poor quality
text: I think they also believe that whatever the AI is giving is crap

Travis had no restrictions - even if you use AI for anything he doesn't mind, but know what you are using it for

Even though designers have their own principles and values I think that thing has changed now

sub: Idealist designer stance no longer viable
text: Nowadays I think that kind of mindset won't work - everybody wants designers to understand from all perspectives

Now I think the larger picture is business - design is one part of it that's enhancing that business

sub: Human refinement of AI drafts required
text: AI can do a good job in giving first or second or third drafts of design but it still has to be refined

sub: AI limitations in replacing design judgment
text: AI still can't replace a lot of things as a designer can do - if language alignment is possible then maybe

sub: AI as time-liberator for creative work
text: Faster results from AI tools means much more time given towards actual designing things

sub: Figma Codex integration as target skill

sub: Skill direction uncertainty amid rapid AI change
text: In terms of future skills right now I'm not aware - there are new things that are always keep coming

sub: Human expertise commands trust over AI
text: If they're really renowned in their field people gonna believe that whatever they are telling is true

sub: Lifelong mastery vs AI knowledge base
text: If they are mastery of their work and have done it their entire life trusting them would be still better than AI

sub: Data volume does not equal mastery
text: AI is newly developed - even though it has more data than humans it doesn't have the mastery of skill

sub: Designers relatively insulated from job loss

sub: Designer plus AI as career sweet spot
